story.headline: FIFA drops World Cup sell-off plan
story.summary: FIFA scrapped a plan to sell private stakes in a new commercial arm holding its tournaments, and Wales became the first association to withdraw support for Infantino's re-election.
story.display_body: FIFA scrapped its most contentious commercial project in years, and its Swiss president, Gianni Infantino, ended the week fighting to keep his job. On 31 July, football's Zurich-based world governing body abandoned a plan — unveiled only days earlier, on 28 July — to move its tournaments into a new commercial company, FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE), and sell a minority stake (reported at up to 21%) to private investors to raise around $4 billion for its 211 member associations. The revolt was near-total: UEFA said all 55 of its European members would oppose it, CONCACAF's 41 members formally rejected it too, and by FIFA's own admission the scheme had "fractured" the game and was no longer viable — so it was killed before any vote. The backlash then turned personal: days later the Football Association of Wales became the first member association to publicly withdraw its support for Infantino's re-election, citing failures of "governance, leadership and judgement," with other associations weighing similar moves.
story.why: Selling equity in the World Cup would have handed private financiers a lasting claim on football's most valuable asset. The opposition — spanning well over half of FIFA's 211 members — and Infantino's rare, humiliating U-turn are the clearest limit yet on how far the sport's Zurich power centre can commercialise the game over its members' objections.

story.headline: Young Boys and Lugano lead Super League
story.summary: Young Boys, Lugano and St. Gallen all won their opening two Swiss Super League matches; reigning champions Thun were thrashed 6-0.
story.display_body: Switzerland's new Super League season is two rounds old and already has a clear pacesetting group: Young Boys, Lugano and St. Gallen have all won both their games. Young Boys — the Bern club that are the competition's record champions — underlined their intent by thrashing last season's fairytale winners Thun 6-0, after opening with a 4-2 win over Sion; Lugano came from a goal down to win 4-1 at Grasshoppers. The early stumbles came from the bigger names: Basel, one of the country's traditional heavyweights, lost 1-0 at Lausanne, while Servette and Luzern both sit pointless after two games. It is far too soon to read a title race — the Swiss top flight runs to next May — but the opening fortnight has already inverted last season's order, with reigning champions Thun among those chasing.
story.why: In a league where a handful of clubs usually dominate, seeing last year's surprise champions hammered and a traditional power beaten inside the first two weekends is a reminder of how unsettled — and open — the Swiss title picture is heading into the autumn.

story.headline: Tour de France Femmes opens in Switzerland
story.summary: The Tour de France Femmes ran its first two stages in Switzerland; Lorena Wiebes won both to take yellow, with Swiss rider Noemi Ruegg fourth overall.
story.display_body: The Tour de France Femmes — the biggest race in women's cycling — began this year on Swiss roads, with its first two stages run entirely in Switzerland before the race crossed into France. Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) dominated the Grand Départ, winning both the opening stage into Lausanne and Sunday's run from Aigle — home of cycling's world governing body, the UCI — along Lake Geneva, and she leads the general classification (the overall time standings) by 14 seconds. The Swiss interest is real: Noemi Rüegg (EF Education-Oatly) climbed to fourth overall, best of the home riders, while Marlen Reusser (Movistar) — one of the world's finest time-triallists (specialists in solo races against the clock) — crashed on stage two but rejoined the main group and sits in a cluster of favourites 20 seconds back. With mountain stages and a time trial still to come in France, the fight for the overall title has barely started.
story.why: A sprinter in yellow after two flat stages is normal; what matters for a non-follower is that the real contenders are still bunched within 20 seconds, so the race is wide open — and that a Swiss rider is sitting inside the top four as it heads for the decisive terrain.

story.headline: Australia top slimmed-down Glasgow Games
story.summary: Australia topped the medal table as a pared-back, roughly ten-sport Commonwealth Games closed in Glasgow on 2 August.
story.display_body: Australia comfortably topped the medal table as the Commonwealth Games closed in Glasgow on 2 August, finishing with roughly 70 golds and about 170 medals in all — well clear of England, second on around 110 medals, and Canada in third. The bigger story was the event itself: this was a deliberately pared-back Games, cut to about ten sports across a handful of venues after the Australian state of Victoria abandoned its hosting deal in 2023 and Glasgow stepped in to stop the Commonwealth Games collapsing entirely. Organisers called the compact model a success and a template for a cheaper future; sceptics counter that a single-city, ten-sport edition still leaves unanswered whether a 90-plus-nation event rooted in the British Empire has a lasting place on the modern sporting calendar. (Switzerland, not a Commonwealth country, does not compete.)
story.why: This was less a contest than a survival exercise for one of world sport's oldest multi-sport events — and it worked, but only by shrinking. The question it leaves is whether "smaller and cheaper" is a genuine future or just a stay of execution.

story.headline: Iran denies US talks Trump calls imminent
story.summary: Iran's foreign ministry denied any talks with the US, hours after Trump claimed a new negotiating round begins Monday and a Hormuz deal is imminent.
story.display_body: Iran's foreign ministry flatly denied on Monday 3 August that any talks with the United States are under way, hours after Donald Trump claimed a new round of negotiations would "begin Monday" and that a deal was "imminent." Trump, who over the weekend said he had called off a planned strike he described as potentially "the biggest attack since World War II," told reporters the emerging deal concerned control of the Strait of Hormuz — the shipping chokehold Iran can throttle — "and ultimately the denuclearisation of Iran." Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei countered: "We are not going to host a delegation or be guests of a country during these days," and both Al Jazeera and Swiss broadcaster SRF report Tehran's own diplomacy is running through Oman on Hormuz shipping security, not directly with Washington. Analysts cited by Al Jazeera noted Iran's wording may leave room for indirect contacts, but cautioned that Trump's repeated pattern of threatening a strike and then cancelling it has eroded his credibility as a negotiator.
story.why: The gap between Trump's "imminent deal" and Iran's on-record denial is the whole story — the US administration has announced a "final" halt or a breakthrough several times in this war without one materialising, so the operative fact today is that the two sides are not, by Iran's account, actually talking.

story.headline: US and Japan jointly prop up the yen
story.summary: Japan and the US confirmed a rare joint intervention, their first since 2011, to lift the yen after it hit 40-year lows.
story.display_body: Japan and the United States confirmed a rare joint intervention to prop up the yen, Tokyo and Washington acknowledged over the weekend of 2 August after the currency touched 40-year lows. The coordinated yen-buying — the first joint action between the two since 2011 — was executed in New York markets last Thursday (30 July), with Tokyo estimated to have sold roughly $59 billion to buy yen; the currency rose as much as 1.4% to about 155.20 per dollar and gained 3.8% over two sessions. Trump framed the US role as a favour — "They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we're always there for Japan" — while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington "strongly support[s] Japan's decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen." A weak yen (a currency intervention means a government buying its own currency to push its value up) had driven up Japan's import prices and inflation, denting household budgets and the prime minister's approval.
story.why: It is highly unusual for the US Treasury to spend to strengthen another country's currency — the last such joint move followed Japan's 2011 earthquake — so the step signals how far the yen's slide had gone and an unusually hands-on US posture on exchange rates.

story.headline: Sudan army drone strike kills 35 in Darfur
story.summary: A Sudanese army drone hit a village community court in North Darfur, killing at least 35, a rights group said.
story.display_body: A Sudanese army drone struck a traditional community court in the village of Garra al-Zawaya, North Darfur, on Sunday 2 August, killing at least 35 people, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said. The strike hit around 1 p.m. local time as villagers gathered under a tree for hearings on local disputes in territory held by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF); a local witness said the dead included four tribal leaders and two RSF commanders. Emergency Lawyers, which documents abuses by both sides, reported the toll. The attack is part of Sudan's three-year war between army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo; the UN says more than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes in the first five months of 2026 alone.

story.headline: Suicide bombing kills 14 in Swat Valley
story.summary: A suicide bomber hit an anti-militant rally outside a police station in Kabal, Swat Valley, killing at least 14.
story.display_body: A suicide bomber killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 22 at an anti-militant rally outside a police station in Kabal, in Pakistan's Swat Valley, on Sunday evening 2 August. The bomber detonated as police tried to stop and search him at the station entrance, striking demonstrators who had gathered to protest a resurgence of violence in Swat — long a stronghold of the Pakistani Taliban (TTP, the domestic insurgency active since 2007). No group claimed responsibility. The bombing followed a drone attack that killed 11 officers days earlier and a July car bombing, claimed by the TTP, that killed 27 soldiers.

story.headline: Lula launches fourth-term bid in Brazil
story.summary: Brazil's Lula launched a fourth-term campaign for October's election, framing it as a fight over national sovereignty amid US tariffs.
story.display_body: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, launched a bid for a fourth term on Sunday 2 August, framing the October 2026 election as a contest over national sovereignty. At a Workers' Party convention in São Paulo, Lula pledged this would be his final term and said Brazil must defend its mineral resources and be ready so "no one invades this country." He is leaning on a nationalist message after the Trump administration imposed two rounds of tariffs on Brazilian goods in July, casting his likely challenger Flavio Bolsonaro — who has close ties to Trump — as beholden to foreign interests. A Datafolha poll put Lula ahead 48% to 43% in a potential runoff, a narrow margin in a polarised country.

story.headline: Cuba suffers another nationwide blackout
story.summary: Cuba's national grid collapsed again on 3 August, at least the fourth total outage this year amid a US oil blockade and ageing plants.
story.display_body: Cuba was plunged into another nationwide blackout on Monday 3 August, its state Electric Union (UNE) said, the latest in a run of total grid failures. It is at least the fourth national outage this year — three struck within nine days in July — as ageing thermoelectric plants, some over 30 years old, buckle from fuel and spare-part shortages. Havana blames a US oil blockade imposed after the 3 January abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, which cut off Cuba's main supplier; independent analysts point to decades of underinvestment and mismanagement as the deeper cause.

story.headline: Heatwave idles Beznau reactors, records fall
story.summary: Switzerland's fourth heatwave of 2026 forced the Beznau nuclear plant to shut both reactors and set temperature records in Ticino.
story.display_body: Switzerland's fourth heatwave of summer 2026 is straining infrastructure, with the Beznau nuclear plant shutting both reactors and Ticino setting fresh temperature records, SRF's live coverage reported on Monday 3 August. Beznau powered down both units because river water had grown too warm to cool them safely; Lugano and Locarno recorded their hottest-ever 1 August; and low water on the Rhine is hampering shipping in the east. Agriculture has been hit hard enough to threaten winter vegetable supplies, and warm conditions are helping the invasive Japanese beetle spread into new areas, with over 60 detected in canton Schwyz.
story.why: The concrete disruptions — a nuclear station idled by warm rivers, record heat in the south, a stressed food supply — show how a run of heatwaves now reaches everyday systems in Switzerland, not just the thermometer.

story.headline: French gangs raid Swiss armouries at pace
story.summary: Fedpol logged 35 armoury burglaries in 2026, run as crime-as-a-service by French networks recruiting minors on social media.
story.display_body: Organised gangs, largely operating out of France, are raiding Swiss gun shops at an alarming pace, with federal police (Fedpol) logging 35 armoury burglaries — 22 of them attempted break-ins — since the start of 2026, Le Temps reported on Monday 3 August. Investigators describe a "crime-as-a-service" model: recruiters advertise on Snapchat, TikTok and Telegram, offering "soldiers" well over €10,000 per robbery to steal weapons. The same French-based networks are tied to a parallel wave of fake-police scams that, since 2022, have produced over 5,000 cases and roughly 18 million francs stolen, concentrated in French-speaking Switzerland.
story.why: A domestic-crime trend the reader would encounter locally, and an example of how social-media recruitment is turning cross-border property crime into an outsourced, industrialised business.
